task:
Design a harness for a **turn-based** game (tier 1: the world waits for the agent).

Game: `Hanabi (offline standard)` — Cooperative standard Hanabi, 2 seats, all controlled by the same policy.
Seat 0 starts; turns advance modulo the number of players. Each color R,Y,G,W,B has
three 1s, two each of 2/3/4, and one 5 (50 cards). Hands contain five cards for 2-3
players, four for 4-5. The TEAM shares eight clue tokens and three lives.
Build each firework in order 1,2,3,4,5. Playing any own card is legal: only the next
required rank succeeds; a duplicate or skipped rank is discarded and loses a life.
A discard restores one clue and is illegal at eight clues. A successful 5 restores
one clue, capped at eight. After a play/discard, draw a replacement if possible.
Clues cost one token, name one color or rank, target another absolute seat, and
must touch at least one card. Every matching card is identified; untouched cards
exclude that attribute. Repeated truthful clues are legal and still cost a token.
The final draw starts exactly N further actions, ending with the drawer's turn.
No replacements are drawn once the deck is empty. Zero lives or 25 points ends
immediately, without a replacement draw. Maximize terminal score 0-25: zero on
life exhaustion, otherwise the sum of the five heights. There are no bonuses.

Choose a dictionary from legal_actions, or use these compact string commands:
PLAY i; DISCARD i; REVEAL_COLOR seat color; REVEAL_RANK seat rank.
Equivalent JSON: {"type":"PLAY","card_index":0},
{"type":"DISCARD","card_index":0},
{"type":"REVEAL_COLOR","target":1,"color":"R"},
{"type":"REVEAL_RANK","target":1,"rank":1}.
Indices are zero-based oldest-to-newest slots; removing a card shifts later slots
left and a replacement is appended. Ranks are 1-5; targets are absolute seats.
NOOP leaves the game unchanged, without passing. Illegal/malformed actions do
not lose a turn: error reports rejection. Use a finite retry budget externally.

Observation fields: rules_version identifies this engine profile; num_players,
observer/current_player and turn identify the current view and valid action count.
fireworks maps colors to heights; information_tokens, life_tokens and deck_size
are public counts. final_turns_remaining is null until the final draw, then N,
decrementing after each subsequent valid action. hands is indexed by absolute seat.
Each card has opaque card_id, current index, color/rank (always null for your own
hand), possible_colors/possible_ranks, and color_clued/rank_clued positive flags.
The Cartesian product of these masks encodes literal positive AND negative clues,
not remaining card availability or conventions. New cards have all candidates.
discard_pile contains public discards/misplays. history contains public actions,
clue touched_card_ids, revealed play/discard faces and drawn_card_id only; it
never gives a drawn face. legal_actions is complete and empty when done.
fireworks_sum measures progress, score is current benchmark score (zero after
bomb-out), done/end_reason indicate terminal state, and error is null or a
rejection diagnostic. At terminal the last actor remains the observer.

Maintain separate private sessions/scratchpads per seat and episode. Never feed
one seat's visible hands or private reasoning to another seat; only public events
and preagreed conventions can be shared. Reset clears engine episode state; the
caller must clear its own sessions. Seeds, deck order and engine internals are
not policy inputs. Shared private memory would make the run omniscient.


Actions:
- PLAY: PLAY i: play own current slot i (may misplay and lose a life).
- DISCARD: DISCARD i: discard own slot i to restore a clue; illegal at eight clues.
- REVEAL_COLOR: REVEAL_COLOR seat color: spend one clue and mark all matches in that other seat's hand.
- REVEAL_RANK: REVEAL_RANK seat rank: spend one clue and mark all matching ranks (1-5).
- NOOP: Do nothing; does not consume a turn. This transport no-op is not a game pass.
(real-time games: ticks apply 'NOOP' until the first action is posted; afterwards a tick without a fresh action repeats the last posted action)
Targets are absolute seat numbers. Card indices are current hand slots. A clue must match at least one card and marks every matching card; untouched cards receive negative information. No pass action exists.

Model available through `ctx`: `ctx.think(prompt, session_id=...)` — Astra (System-2). Budget: 40 calls
per episode; one call may return a plan of several actions. `ctx.act(action)` applies one action and
returns the next observation. Each episode has a wall-clock deadline of 1800 s, including model
latency (`ctx.budget.remaining()["wall_s"]`); when it passes, or the call budget is used up, the episode
ends with the score reached. Each episode starts cold: fresh `ctx.memory` and fresh module globals.

Evaluation: mean score over the training seeds (the game's own score, see the description), then fewer
System-2 calls, then fewer actions. A candidate can only be selected if none of its training episodes
ends with an error (see the contract: e.g. a TimeoutError from a model call that the harness does not
catch).

What the harness must design: how observations are shown to Astra (full history, a diff, an ASCII map
with a legend, only what changed), what to remember between calls (rules learned, states visited,
plans), how to parse Astra's reply into actions robustly, how many actions to commit per call, when
cheap scripted search or bookkeeping replaces a model call, and how to notice that a plan or belief was
wrong. If the description says that rules or action effects are not given, discovering them by
experiment is part of the task.

**Evaluation scope.** The harness is selected on the training seeds of this game and then reported on
unseen seeds of the same game; there is no held-out game. Rules, strategies and search that the game
description or the study establish may be implemented as code once they are verified against
observations — but nothing specific to the training seeds.

## Prior knowledge from the study phase
The study phase researched this game (rules, interface, community strategies). Use it: implement exact
rules, bookkeeping and search as code and put planning and adaptation into Astra prompts — but verify
every claim against observations, because sources can be wrong or outdated for this build of the game.

The full documents are readable in this archive under `prior/` (`prior/strategies.md`, `prior/brief.md`, `prior/interfaces.md`, `prior/study.json`, `prior/ADAPTOR.md`). Below: excerpts within a size budget; every cut is marked `…(truncated; full text in prior/<file>)`.

### study/study.json (summary)
- strategy_summary: Put legality, card multiplicities, positive and negative clue constraints, correlated own-hand beliefs, critical/dead cards, and final-round counting in code. Play cards guaranteed safe by literal information or a precisely shared signaling protocol, and protect threatened last copies needed for reachable color sequences. Evaluate clues by what the recipient can infer and execute before its deadline, balancing saves, safe plays, token recovery and deck progress. Begin with conservative literal clues and a fixed chop/save convention, then test direct play signals and short belief search before adding finesse chains. Astra should choose multi-turn lines and risk tradeoffs from computed candidate summaries; Jev is optional for typed ambiguity or candidate judgments and should not do arithmetic. At one life, uncertain play can erase the entire score, so compare expected terminal values rather than using a fixed confidence threshold. Keep all private memory and hypothetical search observations isolated by seat even though the same agent controls the team.
- scoring: Report raw terminal Hanabi score in 0-25: zero if all three lives are lost, otherwise the sum of the five firework heights. Expose fireworks_sum separately as public progress, since it may remain nonzero on a bomb-out. Use terminal score as the evaluator objective; do not add clue/life bonuses, normalize by reachable ceiling, or sum repeated cumulative scores. If a step reward is needed, use the change in benchmark score, including the negative terminal change on a bomb-out. Verify any substituted engine against this fixed profile.
- interface.observation: Plain JSON for the current absolute seat: rules version, player count, actor/observer, turn, five stack heights, clue/life counts, deck size, final-turn counter, own opaque card IDs and literal clue candidate masks with true faces null, other seats' visible cards, public discards and action history, complete legal action objects, score/progress, done and end reason. Separate literal facts from protocol inference. Never include deck order, RNG state, seed, all-seat private observations, or identities of draws in shared history.
- interface.actions: Choose one object from legal_actions: PLAY or DISCARD with current own card_index, REVEAL_COLOR with absolute target seat and color R/Y/G/W/B, or REVEAL_RANK with absolute target seat and rank 1-5. No pass. Reject illegal actions without mutating the game. Valid plays can fail and consume a life. Step advances synchronously to the next acting seat and returns its redacted observation; terminal states have no legal actions. Optional native HLE mapping must convert action_type fields, relative target_offset and ranks 0-4 explicitly.

### study/strategies.md
# Strategy prior for Hanabi self-play

Optimize **expected terminal team score, 0–25, with zero on life exhaustion**, under each acting seat's information boundary. One shared policy can agree on conventions before the game, but cannot carry another seat's private view into the current seat's reasoning. There is no opponent to defeat and no timing pressure. Astra can reason at every turn; most gains should come from accurate code bookkeeping and a coherent communication policy. Jev is optional, not the engine for arithmetic or multi-turn planning. [S1, S2]

## Evidence status and source map

External access failed during this study; the following are prior-known references, not newly retrieved pages. No claimed score, threshold, or latency below is a measured result. Exact community conventions vary by group and level. The simple protocol proposed below is an **engineering recommendation**, not a claim to reproduce H-Group or an optimal published agent.

* **S1 — Hanabi rules:** https://www.ultraboardgames.com/hanabi/game-rules.php . Actions, information restrictions, multiplicities and ending.
* **S2 — Bard et al., The Hanabi Challenge: A New Frontier for AI Research:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.00506 . Cooperative partial observability, established rule/convention approaches, learned agents, and the difference between self-play and ad-hoc play.
* **S3 — H-Group community conventions:** https://hanabi.github.io/ . Play/save clues, focus, chop, finesse, prompts, tempo and more advanced convention systems. Treat the site as a community reference, not mandatory rules. Deep page locations and current wording were not verified.
* **S4 — Foerster et al., Bayesian Action Decoder for Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.01458 . Action choice communicates information under a common policy; public belief reasoning and conventions.
* **S5 — HLE reference engine:** https://github.com/google-deepmind/hanabi-learning-environment . Legal moves, public/hidden state separation, benchmark mechanics. Its examples are useful baselines, not evidence of optimal strategy.

## Division of work

| Capability | Code | Astra prompts | Jev questions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rules and legality | Authoritative legal actions, counters, masks, score, final-round horizon | Explain a proposed legal move in terms of objective | Never decide legality from intuition |
| Beliefs | Remaining copies, literal clue masks, correlated hand beliefs, feasibility, probabilities | Interpret intentional clues under the fixed protocol; identify competing explanations | Optional classify intent when given already computed features |
| Communication | Stable IDs, shared protocol and separate seat memory, focus/commitment tracking, recipient-perspective simulation | Choose an informative clue or multi-seat sequence and discuss ambiguity | Optional choose among prevalidated clue candidates |
| Tactics | Enumerate legal moves; simulate revealed outcomes; search with information constraints | Trade score, life, clues, deck consumption and turn order | Optional preference among short summaries, never arithmetic |
| Long horizon | Deadline and reachable-score bounds; Monte Carlo estimates if worthwhile | Plan which color dependencies to unlock and which hand to free | Unnecessary |

The harness should receive an observation, calculate exact facts, ask Astra only when there is a meaningful choice, validate the returned action against the current legal list, and execute one turn. Avoid repeated model calls to re-count cards or re-derive token rules. Do not create a hidden fast real-time control loop for this tier-1 task.

## 1. Exact card accounting and literal deduction

**Code; Astra consumes summaries.** Track copies for each identity, successful stacks, public discards including failed plays, visible hands, and own literal constraints. An unplayed card `(c,r)` is immediately playable iff `r == height[c] + 1`. It is already obsolete iff `r <= height[c]`. A higher card is also dead if a required lower rank has no surviving copies anywhere outside the public played/discarded zones. Keep “dead” distinct from “currently unplayable”: a red 4 above a red 1 is often valuable. [S1, S2]

For current seat i, define unseen count `U(c,r) = original copies - successful copies - discarded copies - copies visible in other hands`. Those unseen cards are distributed between i's own hand and the unknown deck. A completed stack contains one successful copy of every rank up to its height. Avoid counting those successful cards again as discarded. Negative U indicates an accounting bug, not a surprising belief.

For each own card maintain the set of identities consistent with **all positive and negative clues** it received while held. Intersect that with physical availability. A clue naming blue removes blue from every untouched card of the target at that moment. It does not constrain future replacements. Track touched IDs and hand shifts exactly. A card need not be fully identified to be safe: if every possible identity is next on its respective stack, it can be played with certainty. Conversely, “rank 1” ceases to imply safe after some colors' 1s have already been played.

Single-card approximation: weight compatible identities by U. For a better belief, enumerate/sample **joint assignments of the entire own hand without replacement**, respecting all masks, with weights proportional to remaining-copy counts at each assignment. Slots are correlated: two cards cannot both be the sole remaining blue 5. An identity feasible for one slot alone may become impossible given the other slots. Deal histories and remembered observations may add legitimate seat-local constraints. Prune impossible assignments before calculating marginals.

For each own slot, calculate `p_playable`, `p_dead`, `p_critical`, likely identities, and guaranteed classifications. These are exact only under an explicitly specified belief model; copy-count priors conditioned solely on clues do not account for all policy-dependent signaling. Do not call a pragmatic inference mathematical certainty. [S2, S4]

**Useful exact examples:**

* Empty stacks and a rank-1 clue: every touched card is playable **now**, but duplicate same-color 1s may make the second one dead after the first play. Recompute after every action.
* Red stack at 2 and both red 3s discarded: red 4/5 are dead and the color's achievable ceiling is 2.
* Red stack at 0 and one red 2 discarded: the other red 2 is critical, even though it cannot yet be played.
* A blue clue touches one of three cards: that card is blue; the two untouched cards are not blue, regardless of whether the intended message was play or save.

## 2. Critical cards, reachable score, and safe discards

**Code for classification and bounds; Astra for tradeoffs.** An unplayed reachable identity is critical when only one physical copy remains outside played/discarded zones. “Only one currently visible” is not the same thing: another may be in the deck or one's own hand. All live 5s begin unique; 2s/3s/4s become unique after one copy is discarded; 1s after two. A unique higher card may stop being valuable after its color is already blocked. [S1, S3]

For each color, find the first missing rank above its height with no surviving copies. Its maximum eventual height is one less than that rank, or 5 if none is missing. Sum these heights for a physical upper bound. This is optimistic: insufficient final turns, inaccessible hands, lives and clue resources can reduce the realizable score further. Discarding the last red 2 can forfeit red 2,3,4,5, not just one point.

Discard preference, subject to the convention's protected cards:

1. Certainly dead/obsolete card, freeing hand space and replenishing a clue.
2. A redundant card when another copy is known to be protected or imminently playable; account for both seats making the same discard decision.
3. Low expected marginal score loss among unprotected cards, considering critical probability, rank dependencies and draw benefit.

Never discard solely because a card is high rank. A unique 5 can wait safely if there is no deadline, and another clue may be needed to preserve it. Also do not reflexively save every 5 at any cost: a save that exhausts clues or blocks immediate progress can be inferior to securing several achievable lower ranks. Save urgency is determined by likely discard timing, not rarity alone. [S3]

## 3. Opening and early-game communication

**Code enumerates truthful clue candidates and touched IDs; Astra chooses the productive sequence.** With empty stacks, rank-1 clues are often efficient because every touched 1 is immediately playable. Prefer clues that create several **usable** plays, unlock different colors, and leave the next seat an informed move. At the initial eight clues, discarding is forbidden in this profile; a clue is often the natural opening. A blind play is a risk, not the default opening. [S1–S3]

Evaluate actionability, not raw number of touched cards. Three 1s containing duplicates are not three guaranteed points. A color clue touching both red 1 and red 4 is ambiguous without a focus convention. Giving information to a later seat may leave the immediate next seat with no safe move and no good token action. In 2-player games, each clue is delivered to the next actor, making simple protocols particularly effective; in 3–5 players, intervening turns and clue urgency matter much more.

Default opening protocol: start with literal clues and a published discard convention; add play/save signaling only once both clue giver and receiver use the same decoder. Do not introduce a finesse spontaneously because Astra notices an attractive line.

## 4. Clue value: actionability, saving, tempo, and negative information

…(truncated; full text in prior/strategies.md)

| Which of these already legal clue candidates is clearest? | Candidate IDs and computed recipient deductions | Advisory selection when no multi-turn planning is needed |
| Does this plan rely on an undeclared convention? | yes/no, with protocol and concise plan | Additional review, not a proof |
| Which candidate needs deeper planning? | Candidate IDs with resource/horizon summaries | Prioritize Astra attention |

Do not ask Jev to count copies, calculate probability, choose legal actions from raw text, maintain convention state, or solve a multi-seat chain. Code should answer exact questions; Astra should handle planning. The tier-1 world waits, so no latency-based reason exists to force a Jev call.

## 11. Common failures and their remedies

There are no adversarial counters in ordinary cooperative Hanabi. The relevant “counters” are responses to resource bottlenecks, ambiguity and inconsistent teammates.

| Failure / bottleneck | Remedy | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Same agent remembers a card face from another seat | Isolate private histories/model sessions by seat; share public transcript only | **Code** |
| Every touched card treated as playable | Separate literal clues, save status and play promises; recompute after each play | **Code + Astra** |
| Contradictory convention interpretations | Freeze protocol and priority rules; downgrade ambiguous clues to literal information | **Code + Astra** |
| Card remembered by stale slot | Track stable IDs, remap action index at decision time | **Code** |
| Duplicate plays after a multi-card 1 clue | Recompute each card against updated stacks and copy beliefs | **Code** |
| Last copy discarded, blocking all higher ranks | Compute critical/dead status and color ceilings before discards; send timely saves | **Code + Astra** |
| Two players discard different copies of the same needed identity | Track imminent partner discards and common protection commitments | **Code + Astra** |
| Zero clues and no known play | Use best legal discard to restore information; avoid arriving here with threatened critical cards | **Astra using code values** |
| Eight clues and no safe play | Give a useful truthful clue, or a safe redundant clue if needed; discard is illegal | **Code + Astra** |
| Over-saving makes every hand protected and stalls draws | Release proven dead cards; define fallback discard by expected loss; balance saves against tempo | **Code + Astra** |
| Misplay based on “high confidence” at one life | Compare expected terminal score including zero on failure | **Code + Astra** |
| Clever finesse recipient cannot decode | Reject unless predeclared rules and turn order justify the same unique interpretation | **Code + Astra; optional Jev review** |
| Late clue reaches a seat after its final turn | Compute exact remaining actor sequence before assessing clue benefit | **Code** |
| Raw own-card unknowns confused with rank zero/one | Normalize external rank encodings and unknown sentinels at the adaptor boundary | **Code** |
| Search plays partners' hidden cards with omniscient knowledge | Restrict each simulated policy to its view; group indistinguishable decision nodes | **Code** |
| Strong training seeds but poor held-out results | Evaluate paired policies on disjoint random deals; report bomb-outs and variance | **Evaluation code** |

## 12. Recommended development order

1. Implement and verify the simulator/interface contract before optimizing play. Reproduce deterministic legal episodes and targeted ending/clue fixtures.
2. Add literal candidate masks, card accounting, dead/critical detection, legal-action validation and seat isolation. Start with guaranteed plays, useful literal clues, and conservative discards.
3. Establish a single common save/chop protocol and endgame countdown; compare behavior over many random seeds. This should eliminate obvious accidental discards and useless late clues.
4. Give Astra concise candidate summaries and recipient-perspective clue assessments. Tune resource/risk choices against terminal score, not clue entropy alone.
5. Test the explicit direct-play signaling extension and short belief rollouts. Add advanced conventions only when failure traces show the baseline's communication limits and all seats can decode the richer protocol.
6. Keep improvements only when paired held-out evaluation supports them; report mean score, spread, bomb-out rate and perfect rate, separated by player count. Evaluate bomb-out handling and information isolation as correctness requirements, not adjustable performance tricks.

No empirical performance target is asserted here. The challenge paper discusses strong established agents [S2], but matching their scores depends on player count, rule profile, convention implementation, inference budget and evaluation seeds.

### study/brief.md
# Hanabi (card game): study brief

Hanabi is a cooperative, hidden-information, turn-based card game for 2–5 players. All seats work toward five ascending fireworks, one in each color, for a maximum score of 25. The requested evaluation controls every seat, but each decision must still use only that seat's permitted information. It is **tier 1**: an offline simulator changes state only when an action is applied. Seconds or minutes of reasoning consume no game time. Evaluator time/call budgets are separate from the rules. [R1, R2, R3]

## Evidence and verification status

This study was prepared on 2026-10-29. Live requests to GitHub, raw.githubusercontent.com, and PyPI failed with `curl: (6) Could not resolve host`. There is no browser/search tool available in this session. The URLs below are source references for subsequent verification, **not pages successfully retrieved during this study**. Rules, interface descriptions, and community conventions below are based on established prior knowledge; package-version details are explicitly provisional. No game-playing code has been written.

Local checks did verify the evaluator interpreter is Python 3.12.3 on linux-x86_64; pip 26.2.2, Python headers, CMake 3.28.3, and g++ 13.3.0 are present. HLE, OpenSpiel, PettingZoo, NumPy, CFFI, setuptools, and wheel are absent from that interpreter. No relevant cached simulator was found in the project, checked temporary paths, or uv cache. See `interfaces.md` for the dependency-free offline choice.

## Standard game, without rainbow or other variants

* Deck: five colors, ranks 1–5; **3 copies of each 1, 2 copies each of 2/3/4, 1 copy of each 5 per color**. Ten cards per color, fifty total.
* Deal five cards per seat with 2–3 players, four with 4–5. Players see everybody else's hand, never the faces of their own cards. Deal and draws are private to the drawer but visible to the other seats. Begin with eight information/clue tokens, three life/fuse tokens, and five empty stacks.
* On a turn, take exactly one action: play an own-hand card; discard an own-hand card to recover a clue token; or spend a clue token to tell one other seat a color or rank present in its hand. Turns advance clockwise.
* A clue must identify **every** matching card and no nonmatching card. It cannot target yourself, identify both rank and color, or name an absent attribute. Untouched cards receive negative information: a red clue excludes red on every other card in that target's current hand.
* A play succeeds only when its rank is exactly one more than that color's current stack height. A failed play removes the card to discards and loses one life. A successful 5 also recovers one clue token, capped at eight.
* Play and discard remove the selected card and draw one replacement if the deck is nonempty. A clue does not draw. Failed plays also draw if the episode has not already ended.
* The recommended HLE-style profile forbids discarding at eight clues, forbids a clue at zero clues, and allows redundant but truthful clues. Some tabletop interpretations differ on discarding at full clues; freeze this profile for evaluation rather than mixing rules.
* Drawing the final deck card starts the final round: **each seat gets one further turn, including the seat that drew it**. The triggering turn is not one of those extra turns. During that round there are no draws and hands can shrink. End earlier on completion of all five stacks or exhaustion of lives. [R1, R2, R3]

## Score and progress

The visible stack total is the sum of the five stack heights, always 0–25. The recommended benchmark terminal score is **0 on loss of the third life, otherwise the stack total**. This makes a bomb-out a loss and follows the commonly used HLE benchmark convention. The physical rules describe the fuse-out as losing; implementations sometimes retain achieved stack points instead. Publish the scoring profile explicitly and check any imported engine before using it. The adaptor should expose both `fireworks_sum` and `score`; report `score` to the evaluator, without normalization, clue bonuses, or survival bonuses. [R1, R3, R4]

During play, stack total measures immediate progress. Remaining copies and the lowest rank permanently lost in each color determine the achievable ceiling. A score of 20 can be an excellent salvage result after a necessary card is lost, but the evaluation objective remains expected terminal score, not percentage of the remaining ceiling. Use score distribution, bomb-out rate, and frequency of 25 only as supplementary diagnostics.

## Controls and pace

Use structured actions, not keyboard or mouse input: `PLAY` with current hand index, `DISCARD` with current hand index, `REVEAL_COLOR` with another seat and color, or `REVEAL_RANK` with another seat and rank. Select from the observation's legal-action list. A valid but incorrect play is an ordinary move with a life penalty; an out-of-range index or illegal clue is an adaptor validation error and must not silently consume a turn. There is no pass action. `interfaces.md` defines exact JSON fields and terminal behavior.

There is **no finite game-imposed decision deadline**. `study.json` uses **`decision_latency_s: -1.0` as a documented sentinel for unbounded latency**, because standard JSON cannot encode infinity. Do not treat it as a negative timeout. Astra may plan on every turn; Jev is optional and unnecessary for timing. An operational timeout such as 60 seconds per reasoning call is a harness budget, not a game rule.

### adaptor/ADAPTOR.md
# Hanabi adaptor

This adaptor is a local, dependency-free Python implementation of the standard Hanabi rules. It runs in-process under the evaluator's Python 3.12 environment and starts no server, GUI, account, or network connection. `make_game()` returns a tier-1 `TurnGame`; `step()` applies one action synchronously and returns the next current-seat observation.

The default profile has two cooperating seats, seat zero starts, five colors (`R`, `Y`, `G`, `W`, `B`), ranks 1-5, card multiplicities 3/2/2/2/1, five-card hands, eight shared clues, and three shared lives. The implementation also accepts `num_players=3`, `4`, or `5` as separately labelled variants (five-card hands for 2-3 seats and four-card hands for 4-5 seats). `EVAL_KWARGS` fixes evaluation at two players. `info()["suite"]` labels the profile as `standard-2p`, etc.; report extension suites separately, never aggregate them into the primary two-player score.

Every reset creates and uniformly shuffles a fresh standard 50-card deck with a private `random.Random(seed)`. The initial multiset is ordered by color R,Y,G,W,B, then rank 1-5, then repeated copies. After Python's shuffle, dealing is round-robin starting at seat 0, popping from the end of the list; replacements also pop from that end. IDs begin at 0 and increment at deal/draw time. Reproducibility is scoped to `hanabi-standard-offline-1` and this Python RNG implementation, not HLE or other engines. All integer seeds are accepted, but the declared disjoint evaluation sets are:

| Split | Seeds | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| train | 11, 12, 13, 14 | Harness tuning |
| dev | 201 | Proposer experiments and local tests |
| validation | 301, 302, 303 | Finalist re-evaluation |
| heldout | 101, 102, 103, 104 | Final reporting |

These seeds were assigned without selecting for favorable outcomes. Seeds appear only in evaluator metadata, never observations or `describe()`. A reset discards all engine history, clues, counters, IDs and diagnostics.

The observation is JSON-safe structured state for the acting absolute seat. Its own cards expose only opaque card IDs and literal candidate color/rank masks; other hands expose their actual faces. Public fireworks, clue/life counts, deck size, discard pile, action history, final-round countdown, and all currently valid action objects are included. A clue updates positive matches and negative exclusions for every card in the target hand. Invalid or malformed actions leave state unchanged and set an `error` field in the next observation.

Actions are dictionaries: `PLAY` or `DISCARD` with `card_index`, or `REVEAL_COLOR` / `REVEAL_RANK` with an absolute `target` and color/rank. Alternatively use `PLAY 0`, `DISCARD 0`, `REVEAL_COLOR 1 R`, or `REVEAL_RANK 1 2`. Verbs and color letters are case-insensitive. `NOOP`, the action-spec no-op, does not advance a turn and is not a game pass. Bare parameterized verbs are rejected. There is no automatic replacement of bad actions; the harness should limit retries. `step()` returns the observation dictionary directly, not a Gym tuple.

Playing the next required rank advances a firework; a misplay loses a life and is discarded. Discards and rank-5 plays recover a clue (capped at eight). Discard is unavailable at eight clues. When the last card is drawn, the triggering action does not consume the countdown; exactly one further action per seat is allowed, unless all lives are lost or all five fireworks reach 5 first. Immediate life-exhaustion/perfect endings omit the useless replacement draw. Terminal observations keep the last actor's masked view and contain no legal actions; further steps do nothing.

`score` reports the fireworks sum during play and at a normal terminal, or zero when all lives are exhausted. Evaluate the final value once; do not sum cumulative scores. `fireworks_sum` is exposed separately in observations and `score_breakdown()` so progress remains visible after a bomb-out. `info()["reward"]` is the change in benchmark score on the last accepted step, including the negative change on a bomb-out; rejected actions and no-ops set it to zero. `score_breakdown()` also reports clue/life counts as diagnostics, not objective bonuses. Gameplay failures are valid trials; no external infrastructure is used. `info()["valid_trial"]` is therefore true.

The adaptor emits only the current seat's view and owns no policy sessions or private policy memory. The harness MUST route observations by `observer` into separate per-seat sessions and scratchpads, and clear them at every reset. Shared memory may contain only public events and preagreed conventions. A single accumulated transcript containing different seats' private views makes this centralized/omniscient play and must not be reported as standard hidden-information Hanabi. The adaptor cannot erase the caller's memory or sandbox Python introspection; policy code must not access engine fields, evaluator seed metadata, or the seed declarations. No built-in opponent, bot, convention, or open-hand mode is provided.

No credentials or environment variables are required; `env.example` is intentionally empty of mandatory values. `requirements.txt` documents that there are no additional dependencies to install. The game performs no file writes, downloads, telemetry, or background work. `close()` is idempotent; no external resources need releasing. Verification artifacts live under `runtime/`, which the source hash skips.
